title: The Fixed-Income Couple
file: Robert: Social Security plus a small pension. Linda: part-time work
Linda has a $50,000 group policy through her employer
None set aside for final expenses
Two grown children, three grandchildren out of state
Robert takes medication for blood pressure. Linda is healthy
story: Robert retired last year. Linda still works a few days a week and expects to stop at 65, like Robert. When you ask about coverage, Linda says, "I have my policy through work, so we are covered." Robert adds, "We do not have any savings put aside, and we do not want the kids stuck paying for our funerals."
prompt: Build your angle. Choose the strongest logical reasons, the strongest emotional reasons, and the best response to the objection.

groups.label: Logical reasons
groups.hint: Pick the two facts from their situation that make the strongest case on paper.

options.t: They have no savings set aside, so the funeral and final bills would come out of their children's pockets.
options.why: This is the actual problem they named. A policy sized to the bill is a direct answer to it.

options.t: Linda's work policy will usually end when she retires, so the $50,000 goes away just as her paycheck does.
options.why: The coverage they are counting on is tied to her job. It is temporary, and it disappears at the moment they most need a plan.

options.t: Final costs keep rising, so a level monthly payment now beats a one-time bill later.
options.why: A reasonable point, but general. It is not tied to what this couple told you.

options.t: They should invest the premium in the stock market instead.
options.why: Not a fit. It ignores that they have no savings and need a bill covered, and it steers away from your product without an honest comparison.

options.t: The kids' college costs need to be covered.
options.why: Their children are grown. This shows you were not listening.

options.t: Robert's blood pressure could affect his rates or approval later, so it is better to apply now while he qualifies.
options.why: True and relevant, but secondary to the two main gaps.

groups.label: Emotional reasons
groups.hint: Pick the two that connect to what they actually want and worry about, without pressure or fear tactics.

options.t: Point out how sad it would be for the grandchildren to see their grandparents leave nothing behind.
options.why: Manipulative, fear-based, and not grounded in anything they said.

options.t: They will likely want a policy at least as large as the $50,000 Linda has now, so the peace of mind she feels today does not shrink.
options.why: Anchors the recommendation to a number and a feeling they already know.

options.t: Robert said he does not want the kids stuck with the bill. This plan lets their kids remember them, not the invoice.
options.why: Strong and in his own words, but the top two connect to their specific timing and situation.

options.t: Suggest that good spouses always buy insurance.
options.why: A guilt trip. It puts pressure on their relationship instead of on their situation.

options.t: Bring up the trip to visit the grandchildren that they can finally afford.
options.why: Not connected to the need and drifts away from the problem.

options.t: Linda will likely retire at 65 like Robert, and the safety net she has today disappears when the paycheck does.
options.why: Ties the timing of her retirement to a moment they can picture, without pushing fear.

groups.label: Likely objection
groups.hint: They say: "We are on a fixed income. We cannot afford anything new."

options.t: "You cannot afford not to. What will your kids do?"
options.why: Pressure and guilt. It hardens the objection.

options.t: "Okay, call me if things change."
options.why: Gives up on the sale and on the couple.

options.t: "Fixed income is exactly why this matters. A small, level payment now replaces a large bill later. Let us find an amount that fits your monthly budget."
options.why: Agrees with the concern, turns it into the reason, and offers a way to make it fit.

options.t: "It is only about a couple of dollars a day, that is nothing."
options.why: Dismisses a real budget limit and skips the reason they need it.

title: Run the Appointment
file: First in-home appointment with a senior prospect
Leave with an application or a firm next step
story: Top final expense agents run the appointment in the same shape every time. These five steps are out of order.
prompt: Put the steps in the order you would run them. Use the arrows to move a step up or down.

steps.t: Estimate what final costs might be and what is already covered, to show the gap
steps.why: A number the client agrees with is what makes the recommendation feel earned.

steps.t: Present the plans they qualify for, with price and how each pays out, and complete the application
steps.why: You can only present the right plan once you know what they qualify for.

steps.t: Greet them warmly, set the agenda and confirm what they would like to leave with
steps.why: A shared agenda lowers resistance to the questions that follow.

steps.t: Ask the health questions to see which type of plan they qualify for
steps.why: Health answers decide between a level benefit from day one and a graded benefit.

steps.t: Ask about their wishes, who will handle arrangements, and any coverage or prepaid plan they have
steps.why: Discovery comes before any numbers.

title: Questions That Find the Need
file: Two adult children, one out of state
story: You are ten minutes in with a couple who are friendly but have not yet said what they want. You want questions that help them see the need for themselves.
prompt: Select every question worth asking. Questions that lead, pressure or anchor on price cost points.

options.t: You do not want to leave your kids stuck with the bill, do you?
options.why: A leading, guilt-heavy question.

options.t: Who would you want to receive this money, and what would you like it to do for them?
options.why: Turns the plan into something they want.

options.t: If something happened to one of you, who would take care of the arrangements and the bills?
options.why: Shows where the burden would land.

options.t: What money could be used right away, and would your family have to wait to reach it?
options.why: Uncovers the timing problem: bills come due before accounts open.

options.t: Have you thought about what you would want for your arrangements, burial or cremation, and whether you would want a service?
options.why: Opens the topic in their words and starts the cost conversation.

options.t: Would you rather I just show you the cheapest thing I have?
options.why: Invites a price-only decision.

options.t: Do you have any life insurance or a prepaid funeral plan already? What does it pay for?
options.why: You cannot size a gap without knowing what is in place.

options.t: What is your monthly budget? Give me a number and I will work backward.
options.why: Budget-first anchors on price before the need is clear.

title: The Cremation Wish
file: Two adult children, one 30 minutes away
"I do not want anyone fussing over me."
story: Lorraine says, "I just want to be cremated. No service, no fuss. That costs almost nothing, so I do not need any insurance." You know cremation still has real costs.
prompt: Build your angle. Choose the strongest logical reasons, the strongest emotional reasons, and the best response to the objection.

groups.label: Logical reasons
groups.hint: Pick the two facts from their situation that make the strongest case.

options.t: Her no-service wish is easier to carry out when the money is set aside and someone knows the plan.
options.why: Real, and it links to her own wishes.

options.t: Every funeral home charges the same for cremation, so she does not need to check.
options.why: Not true. Prices vary.

options.t: She should buy a large policy so her children receive an inheritance.
options.why: She has not asked for that, and it does not fit her income.

options.t: Her family would have to pay first and wait, or draw down her $4,200 checking account, which is her living cushion.
options.why: Shows where the money would come from without a plan.

options.t: Even a simple cremation has costs: the provider's fee, transport, permits, death certificates and a container. A written quote from a funeral home shows the real number.
options.why: Turns "almost nothing" into a specific figure she can see.

options.t: Many plans have a level premium that does not rise, so the price at her age is set from the start.
options.why: True, but generic.

groups.label: Emotional reasons
groups.hint: Pick the two that connect to what they actually want and worry about, without pressure or fear.

options.t: She said "no fuss." A small plan is how she gets it: nobody has to guess, argue or find the money.
options.why: Uses her own words and offers the result she wants.

options.t: Say she is being selfish by not planning.
options.why: Judgmental and it ends the conversation.

options.t: She sounds independent. A plan lets her keep making the decisions.
options.why: A real point, but secondary.

options.t: Her children can grieve without a bill or a phone call to the funeral home. She gives them that ease.
options.why: Ties the plan to a gift for her kids.

options.t: Tell her that no service would break her children's hearts.
options.why: Guilt about a wish she is entitled to.

groups.label: Likely objection
groups.hint: She says: "It costs almost nothing. I do not need insurance."

options.t: "It does cost less than a traditional funeral, and there are still real costs. Let us get a written quote from the funeral home and see what the number looks like."
options.why: Agrees with the true part and offers a way to check.

options.t: "You will regret not planning."
options.why: A scare tactic.

options.t: "Trust me, it costs more than you think."
options.why: Right but unsupported.

options.t: "Cremation is not free."
options.why: Correct but blunt.

title: Which Benefit Fits?
file: Well-controlled blood pressure. No heart, cancer or stroke history
Simplified issue with a level benefit from day one. Guaranteed issue with a graded benefit. Term to age 80
story: Roy is nervous about answering health questions. He asks, "Is there something where I do not have to answer any questions?"
prompt: Which recommendation fits Roy best?

options.t: Guaranteed issue whole life with a graded benefit. It skips the health questions he is nervous about and still covers the full $10,000 he wants.
options.why: It would work, but it costs more for less in the first two years. It is a fallback, not the first choice.

options.t: Whichever of the three plans pays the highest commission, since all three would cover the $10,000 he wants within his budget.
options.why: A recommendation must be based on the client's needs.

options.t: A term policy to age 80 sized to the $10,000 final expense, since term has the lowest monthly premium of the three options.
options.why: Term expires. Final costs come at the end of life, and he could outlive the term with nothing.

options.t: Simplified issue whole life with a level benefit from day one, after going through the health questions with him to confirm he qualifies.
options.why: His health is good. He likely qualifies for full coverage from day one at a lower price than guaranteed issue. Explain that the questions are the way to get there.

title: The Widower
file: Two adult children (Karen, 44 and David, 41), four grandchildren
Social Security plus a $1,400 monthly pension
Type 2 diabetes managed with medication, non-smoker
"I do not want to be a burden."
story: Walter paid for his wife's funeral out of pocket and remembers how hard it was. He says, "I do not want my kids to go through what I did." Then he adds, "With my diabetes, nobody will insure me anyway."
prompt: Build your angle. Choose the strongest logical reasons, the strongest emotional reasons, and the best response to the objection.

groups.label: Logical reasons
groups.hint: Pick the two facts from their situation that make the strongest case on paper.

options.t: Final expense plans are built for his age, and depending on the plan, health questions are simple or not required.
options.why: Answers his belief that he cannot get covered, without promising an outcome.

options.t: Explain how a graded death benefit works in the first couple of years, so nothing is a surprise later.
options.why: An honest disclosure. It builds trust and prevents a claim-time surprise.

options.t: His diabetes will not matter at all and he will be approved automatically.
options.why: Misleading. Approval and terms depend on the plan and its underwriting.

options.t: Price goes up as he ages, so a policy now costs less than the same policy later.
options.why: True, but generic.

options.t: Recommend $250,000 so his kids receive a real inheritance.
options.why: The need is final expenses. The amount does not fit his income or his request.

options.t: His $9,000 in savings is his cushion for living expenses. A right-sized policy keeps that money his and still covers the bill.
options.why: Shows him what the policy protects: his own security.

groups.label: Emotional reasons
groups.hint: Pick the two that connect to what they actually want and worry about, without pressure or fear tactics.

options.t: He can leave a small gift for each grandchild.
options.why: A nice touch, but not what he is worried about.

options.t: Remind him that he is getting older and time is running out.
options.why: Fear-based.

options.t: The dignity of leaving things in order: he chooses the arrangements and his children can simply grieve together.
options.why: Speaks to who he wants to be for his family.

options.t: His kids will resent him if he does not buy this.
options.why: Invented and manipulative.

options.t: Say his late wife would have wanted him to buy it.
options.why: Invoking a deceased spouse to pressure him crosses a line.

options.t: He already lived this with his wife's funeral. Give him the chance to make it easier for Karen and David: no scramble, no decisions, no bill.
options.why: Uses his own experience and offers relief.

groups.label: Likely objection
groups.hint: He says: "My kids can handle it. They are doing fine."

options.t: "Are you sure you want them to struggle?"
options.why: Guilt.

options.t: "Okay. Let me know if that changes."
options.why: Drops the topic and the client.

options.t: "Kids always say that and then cannot pay."
options.why: A guess about his children, and dismissive.

options.t: "I am sure they would do it gladly. That is the point of a small plan: they can do it without the cost or the stress, and you keep your savings."
options.why: Respects his kids and reframes the plan as a gift to them.

title: Declined Elsewhere
file: COPD on an inhaler and Type 2 diabetes. Declined for a policy by another company last month
"I do not want Maria to lose the house paying for my funeral."
story: Carlos is discouraged. He says, "I got turned down last month. I guess nobody will insure me." You know that some plans are guaranteed issue: no health questions, with a graded benefit.
prompt: Build your angle. Choose the strongest logical reasons, the strongest emotional reasons, and the best response to the objection.

groups.label: Logical reasons
groups.hint: Pick the two facts from their situation that make the strongest case.

options.t: A guaranteed issue plan asks no health questions, so his COPD and diabetes do not stop him from qualifying.
options.why: Answers the belief that nobody will insure him.

options.t: He should know the graded benefit up front: if he dies of natural causes in the first two years, beneficiaries typically get premiums paid plus interest. Accidental death is usually paid in full.
options.why: Honest disclosure of the tradeoff. It builds trust and avoids a claim-time surprise.

options.t: We work with a range of carriers, and some of them accept conditions like diabetes and COPD every day. That is exactly why it matters to work with an agent who knows how to underwrite the case and shop it across enough companies to get him qualified for the best plan available at his age.
options.why: Reframes being declined once as a single company's answer, not the industry's, and positions you as the underwriting expert who finds the fit.

options.t: The price is based on age, so applying at 57 costs less than waiting.
options.why: True, but secondary.

options.t: A smaller amount sized to a funeral estimate keeps the premium affordable on $2,300 a month.
options.why: Fits the plan to his budget.

options.t: The graded period does not matter, because most people live more than two years.
options.why: Minimizing a disclosure is not acceptable.

options.t: Because he was declined once, no company will ever cover him again.
options.why: False. It closes a door that is open.

groups.label: Emotional reasons
groups.hint: Pick the two that connect to what they actually want and worry about, without pressure or fear.

options.t: Say Maria could end up homeless.
options.why: A scare tactic.

options.t: His daughter will not have to take on the bills.
options.why: Relevant, but Maria is his main concern.

options.t: He said he does not want Maria to lose the house paying for his funeral. A plan means she never has to choose.
options.why: Uses his own concern and offers relief.

options.t: Tell him time is running out, given his lungs.
options.why: Fear about his health.

options.t: Being turned down probably left him feeling shut out. Show him there is a way to say yes.
options.why: Speaks to the discouragement he just showed you.

groups.label: Likely objection
groups.hint: He says: "If I die in the first two years, they do not pay? That sounds like a scam."

options.t: "It is not a scam. These plans are regulated."
options.why: True but not enough.

options.t: "That is a fair reaction. It is called a graded benefit. In the first two years the plan typically returns what you paid plus interest, and after that it pays the full amount. Accidents are paid in full from day one. It is how they can accept everyone. Let us read it together in the policy."
options.why: Takes the concern seriously, explains it plainly and points to the document.

options.t: "Every plan for people like you works this way."
options.why: Not accurate, and it dismisses his reaction.

options.t: "You will not die in two years."
options.why: You cannot know that.

title: The Caregiver
file: Son, 27, has a disability and lives with her. He receives SSI and Medicaid. No other children nearby
$10,000 through her employer, which ends if she leaves
"If I go first, who takes care of everything for him?"
story: Denise cares for her son every day. She says, "I do not want him to be the one who has to deal with any of this." You know that SSI and Medicaid are means-tested. In most states a person on SSI can hold only $2,000 in countable assets, and money left directly to him could put those benefits at risk. You are not an attorney, so you cannot advise on the legal fix, but you can raise the issue and point her to one.
prompt: Build your angle. Choose the strongest logical reasons, the strongest emotional reasons, and the best response to the objection.

groups.label: Logical reasons
groups.hint: Pick the two facts from their situation that make the strongest case.

options.t: Her work policy ends if she leaves the job, while a personal plan is hers to keep.
options.why: True and relevant, but secondary.

options.t: Arrangements and final bills would fall to someone, and without money set aside that could be her son or other relatives.
options.why: Names the real burden she fears.

options.t: She does not need to plan, because her son's benefits will pay for her funeral.
options.why: False. His benefits are a small monthly amount for living costs. They do not pay for a funeral, and they end when the benefits do.

options.t: At 54, the price is lower than it will be later.
options.why: True, but generic.

options.t: Who she names as beneficiary matters. SSI and Medicaid limit him to about $2,000 in assets, so a $10,000 payout left straight to him would put him roughly $8,000 over the limit. He could lose his monthly check and his health coverage until the money is spent down. An attorney can set up a special needs trust to receive the money instead.
options.why: The strongest angle in the file. It shows you understand the $2,000 asset limit, why a lump sum can cost him more than it gives, and that the fix (a special needs trust) belongs with an attorney, not you.

options.t: Just name her son directly as beneficiary. It is the simplest way.
options.why: This is the mistake the whole puzzle is about. A lump sum paid to him counts against the $2,000 asset limit, can suspend SSI and Medicaid, and skips advice she needs. The money meant to protect him could end up costing him his benefits.

options.t: The benefit limit is high enough that a $10,000 payout will not matter to his benefits.
options.why: False. The SSI asset limit is about $2,000 for one person, so $10,000 is far over it.

groups.label: Emotional reasons
groups.hint: Pick the two that connect to what they actually want and worry about, without pressure or fear.

options.t: She can stop lying awake over it.
options.why: Comforting, but less specific.

options.t: Warn her that she is running out of time.
options.why: A fear tactic.

options.t: She has given years of care. This is one last piece of care that she can put in place now.
options.why: Recognizes what she has done.

options.t: Remind her that her son would be helpless without her.
options.why: Cruel and untrue. He is capable of much, and this is about setting things up so the money helps him instead of hurting his benefits.

options.t: Her worry is who takes care of everything for her son. A plan lines up both the money and the right person, and set up correctly it helps him instead of putting his benefits at risk.
options.why: Speaks to what she said and turns the asset-limit issue into reassurance rather than fear.

groups.label: Likely objection
groups.hint: She says: "I can barely make ends meet. I cannot add another bill."

options.t: "Then I will call you when things improve."
options.why: Drops the need.

options.t: "It is only a few dollars a day."
options.why: Minimizes a real limit.

options.t: "Then let us work backward from what fits. A smaller plan can still cover the basics, and we can choose an amount you can keep without strain. I do not want you to lapse."
options.why: Takes the budget seriously and protects her from a lapse.

options.t: "You cannot afford not to."
options.why: Pressure.

title: Let Me Think About It
file: Widowed, one son who lives nearby
$10,000 whole life, level from day one, $64 a month
story: You presented the plan. Nadine nods along and says, "This all makes sense. I just need to think about it."
prompt: What do you say?

options.t: Say she is getting older and the price will go up, so she should decide today.
options.why: Age does affect price, but urgency in place of explanation feels like pressure.

options.t: Say: "No problem, I will call you next month."
options.why: A month is long enough for the urgency to fade, and you never learn her concern.

options.t: Say: "Of course. What would you like to think through: the amount, the monthly cost, or something else?"
options.why: "Think about it" usually hides a specific concern. A gentle, specific question brings it out so you can address it now.

options.t: Say: "Sure. Can we hold 15 minutes Thursday to go over anything that comes up? I will send the summary tonight."
options.why: Keeps momentum with a next step, but you still do not know the concern.

title: Let Me Talk to My Kids
file: Three adult children. Daughter Renee helps with her bills
$12,000 whole life, level from day one, $79 a month
story: Gloria has been nodding through the whole presentation. Then she says, "I want to run this by Renee first. She helps me with my money."
prompt: How do you respond?

options.t: Hand her your card, tell her there is no rush at all, and ask her to call you once she and Renee have had a chance to talk it over.
options.why: You give away the follow-up and the sale.

options.t: Offer to email the full quote to Renee tonight so she can look it over on her own time, then call both of them next week to answer any questions and finish up.
options.why: Gets the plan in front of both, but a week is long and nobody is there to answer questions.

options.t: Say: "That makes sense. Renee is part of this. Could she join us on a 15-minute call tomorrow evening? I will send a one-page summary you can both keep."
options.why: Respects who she trusts, brings Renee in quickly, and books a specific next step. Gloria still makes the decision.

options.t: Tell her grown children often talk parents out of good decisions, so it is better to finish the application today while you are here.
options.why: Undermines her family and pressures her. It also raises questions about your motives.

title: I Can Get It Cheaper Elsewhere
file: $10,000 whole life, level from day one, $74 a month
What the mailer does not say
Guaranteed issue with a graded benefit for the first two years
story: Vernon pulls a mailer from his pocket. He says, "I can get the same $10,000 for $39 a month. Why would I pay you $74?"
prompt: What do you say?

options.t: Offer to lower his coverage from $10,000 to $5,000 so your monthly price comes in closer to the mailer, and keep everything else the same.
options.why: Matching a number without checking what the mailer offers cuts his coverage for no good reason.

options.t: Say: "Good to compare. May I see it? Let us check that they match: graded or full from day one, a level premium, and the carrier. If theirs is the better fit for you, take it."
options.why: Invites the comparison, points to the real differences and stays honest. He trusts you more for it.

options.t: Say that quality costs a little more, and that unlike a company that sends mailers, you will be personally around to help his family through every step when it is time to file a claim.
options.why: Service matters, but it does not address the price gap with facts.

options.t: Tell him those mailers are usually scams run by companies that never pay, so he should throw it away and stick with a real agent.
options.why: Untrue as a blanket claim, and it insults his judgment.

title: I Am Too Old
file: To help her daughter with final costs
story: Alma tells you, "I am too old for insurance. Nobody will sell it to me at my age."
prompt: What do you say?

options.t: Say: "Good news. At your age, everyone gets approved for the full amount right away, so there is really nothing to worry about."
options.why: False. Older applicants often have a graded benefit.

options.t: Say: "I can certainly check that for you, but at 82 with diabetes and high blood pressure, I would not expect much. Let us see what comes back before you get your hopes up."
options.why: Honest but discouraging, and it does not help her understand her options.

options.t: Say: "You may have more choices than you think. Many plans accept people into their 80s. Let me show you how they work, including any waiting period, so you can decide."
options.why: Corrects the belief, includes the honest tradeoff, and leaves the decision to her.

options.t: Say: "You are probably right. Most companies stop at 80, so it is likely too late, but thank you for being honest with me."
options.why: Gives up on a client who may qualify.

title: I Do Not Trust Insurance Companies
file: His brother's claim was denied years ago after months of delays
story: Earl folds his arms. "Insurance companies take your money and never pay. My brother went through it."
prompt: What do you say?

options.t: Say: "Everyone seems to have a bad story like that, but the truth is that the vast majority of claims get paid without any problem at all, so I would not let one bad experience stop you."
options.why: Dismisses his experience with a generalization.

options.t: Say: "I completely understand, and I promise you that would never happen with my company. We pay every single claim, every time."
options.why: A promise you cannot make.

options.t: Say: "I am sorry that happened. Can you tell me what the reason was? Let me show you how this policy pays and what could cause a claim to be denied, so nothing is a surprise."
options.why: Listens first, treats the story as real, and answers with specifics and transparency.

options.t: Say: "With respect, that is not true. Insurance companies are heavily regulated, and they cannot simply refuse to pay."
options.why: Argues with a story about his own family.

title: I Have Savings in the Bank
file: $18,000 in a savings account in her name alone
story: Mavis says, "I have money put away. I do not need any insurance."
prompt: What do you say?

options.t: Say: "It sounds like you are well prepared, so you probably do not need me. I will leave my card in case anything changes."
options.why: Gives up without exploring the need.

options.t: Say that savings are risky, can run out faster than people expect, and that a policy is the only safe way to cover a funeral.
options.why: Vague, and it dismisses what she has done.

options.t: Say that an account in her name alone may be tied up until her estate is settled, which could delay paying the funeral home and other bills while her children wait for the paperwork to clear.
options.why: A useful point, but it is a statement and not a question, and it is only part of the picture.

options.t: Ask: "That is smart. What is that money for: your everyday safety net, or the funeral? And how would your children reach it quickly? If a policy pays the bill, your savings stay yours."
options.why: Respects her savings, opens up their purpose and the access question, and frames the plan as protecting her money.

title: The Price Stall
story: Both spouses agreed they want to cover their final costs. Then the husband looks at the quote and says, "That is more than I expected."
prompt: Write what you would say next in 2 to 5 sentences. Aim to earn agreement, not to push.

rubric.label: Acknowledges the concern
rubric.tip: Start by showing you heard him. People stop pushing back once they feel understood.

rubric.label: Ties the cost to what is protected
rubric.tip: Bring it back to the reason they wanted coverage: the people they would spare from the bill.

rubric.label: Puts the price in perspective
rubric.tip: Reframe $74 a month as a small daily cost next to a large one-time bill.

rubric.label: Offers a way to fit the budget
rubric.tip: Give them a choice, such as a lower amount, so "too much" has a solution.

rubric.label: Asks for a decision or next step
rubric.tip: Finish with a clear ask. Without it the conversation drifts.

sample: I understand, and I want this to fit your budget. For about $2.50 a day, your children never have to pay for a funeral out of their own pockets. If that still feels like too much, we can lower the amount a little and adjust later. Which would you like to try so we can get your application started today?

title: The Truck Payment
file: Whole life, $15,000 face, bought in 1989. Premium $68 a month
$5,400 left. $312 a month, 18 payments to go
$3,600 a month, Social Security and pension
Dennis takes blood pressure and cholesterol medication. Carol is healthy
$20,000 whole life, level from day one, $88 a month

options.t: Compare the carriers' ratings, benefit types and guaranteed premiums in writing.
options.why: Ensures the two plans are compared like for like.

options.t: Have the new policy approved and in force before cancelling the old one.
options.why: Gene keeps his coverage if the new application does not go through.

options.t: Explain that the new policy starts a new contestability period, and check what the current policy has already satisfied.
options.why: A real tradeoff, and honest disclosure.

options.t: Do not mention the new contestability period, so they do not hesitate.
options.why: Withholding a material fact.

options.t: Cancel the old plan first to save the $96.
options.why: If the new plan is declined he has no coverage.

options.t: Give a written side-by-side comparison and the state replacement notice.
options.why: Required in most states.

groups.label: Likely objection
groups.hint: Loretta says: "We already own this. Why switch to save twelve dollars?"

options.t: "You will regret keeping it."
options.why: A scare tactic.

options.t: "Fair question. The twelve dollars is the smaller part. You would also get $4,000 more coverage and a stronger company, if approved. If the numbers do not clearly win, keep what you have."
options.why: Gives the full picture and offers an honest out.

options.t: "It adds up to $144 a year."
options.why: True but only part of the story.

options.t: "You should always switch when there is a better deal."
options.why: A blanket rule, and it is not helpful.

title: Say This, Not That
file: Presenting a final expense plan at the kitchen table
Nothing you say can be misleading
story: A client asks you a string of questions while you go over the plan. Your license and their trust ride on how you answer.
prompt: Select every statement that is safe to say. Misleading claims cost points.

options.t: Approval depends on your answers to the health questions, so I cannot promise which plan you will get until we go through them.
options.why: Honest about what is not yet known.

options.t: You will definitely be approved, no matter what your health is.
options.why: Only guaranteed issue plans promise acceptance, and they carry a graded benefit.

options.t: This is an investment that will pay you back more than you put in.
options.why: Final expense insurance is protection, not an investment.

options.t: This price is only good until midnight tonight.
options.why: False urgency is a pressure tactic.

options.t: The premium is level and will not go up as you get older, as shown on the application.
options.why: Accurate and matches the paperwork.

options.t: Cancel your old policy today. This one is better.
options.why: Replacement without a full comparison can leave the client worse off and is a compliance risk.

options.t: I can show you quotes from two carriers so you can compare price and benefits.
options.why: Comparison helps the client choose with confidence.

options.t: On this plan, if death is from natural causes in the first two years, the benefit is the premiums paid plus interest. Accidental death is paid in full.
options.why: A plain explanation of a graded benefit.

title: The Final Close
file: Blood pressure controlled with medication. Qualifies for a level benefit from day one
$12,000 whole life, level from day one, $84 a month
story: Frances has told you she wants her children spared from paying for her funeral. She says, "So what would you recommend?"
prompt: Write your closing statement in 3 to 6 sentences: recap what you heard, make your recommendation, set honest expectations, and ask for the application.

rubric.label: Recaps her situation
rubric.tip: Mirror back what she told you so she hears her own reasons.

rubric.label: Makes a clear recommendation
rubric.tip: She asked what you recommend. Say it in one confident sentence.

rubric.label: Connects it to what she wants
rubric.tip: Link the plan to her goal: her children never have to pay.

rubric.label: Sets honest expectations
rubric.tip: Tell her what happens next, such as the health questions and the review, without promising an outcome.

rubric.label: Asks for the application
rubric.tip: End with a direct ask so the conversation turns into action.

sample: Frances, you told me you want your children spared from paying for your funeral, and the home's quote is $9,800 with only about $2,000 in savings. I recommend the $12,000 plan at $84 a month, which is level and pays in full from day one, if you qualify. We will go through a few health questions and the company will review your answers, and I will walk you through each step so there are no surprises. Are you ready to get the application started today?

title: The Lapsed Policy
file: Oxford life policy, $1,700. She knows it is not enough for the funeral she wants
COPD, on oxygen. Cancer a year ago. Stroke 6 months ago. Diabetes
An AmAm policy bought a few months ago from another agent, because she wanted more coverage
You call the carrier to confirm the details. They tell you the policy lapsed the month after it was written
Her health questions were answered incorrectly. The policy would not have paid a claim
story: Rita believed she had two policies. She did not know that the second one lapsed, or that the health answers on the application were wrong. You are the second agent she has talked to about this. Agents who write a policy with false health answers just to get an approval are a common problem in this business, and the person who pays for it is the client. A policy with incorrect answers can be refused at claim time, no matter how long she paid.
prompt: Decide how you handle this appointment. Build your angle, and choose the steps that protect Rita and keep you honest.

groups.label: Logical reasons
groups.hint: Pick the two facts that should drive your recommendation.

options.t: The AmAm policy lapsed, so she has no more coverage than she had before she bought it.
options.why: True and urgent, but on its own it does not explain why the policy was never going to pay.

options.t: A plan bought now costs less than one bought next year.
options.why: True, but generic. It is not why she needs this.

options.t: The health answers on that application were wrong. A carrier can refuse to pay a claim over incorrect answers, so her family could have paid premiums and still received nothing.
options.why: The core lesson. A policy is only worth what it will actually pay, and it pays only when it is underwritten on true answers.

options.t: No carrier will cover someone with her health, so there is nothing more she can do.
options.why: False. Guaranteed issue plans accept applicants regardless of health, with a waiting period before the full benefit.

options.t: The $1,700 from her Oxford policy covers only a small part of the funeral she wants, and the rest would fall on her family.
options.why: The real need, and the reason she called in the first place.

options.t: She can reapply with the same answers. Carriers rarely check.
options.why: Falsifying an application is misrepresentation. It can void the policy and put your license at risk.

groups.label: Emotional reason
groups.hint: Pick the one that connects to what she wants and worries about, without pressure or fear.

options.t: Remind her that at 78 with her health, she may not be here much longer.
options.why: A fear tactic, and cruel.

options.t: She wants her family to have the funeral she planned without scrambling for money. A plan that is real, and that she can count on, does that.
options.why: Speaks to what she wants, and to the fact that she has already been let down once.

options.t: She will sleep better once it is off her mind.
options.why: Comforting, but generic.

options.t: Tell her the last agent was dishonest and that you are the only one who will look out for her.
options.why: Blame and pressure. Let the facts and your honesty speak for you.

options.t: She has had a hard year. She deserves someone who tells her the truth about where she stands.
options.why: Warm and true, but it does not connect to her funeral wishes.

groups.label: Before you recommend it
groups.hint: Pick the two steps that matter most before you write anything.

options.t: Do not mention the lapsed policy. She has enough to worry about.
options.why: She has a right to know what she does and does not have. Silence leaves her exposed.

options.t: Tell her plainly that the AmAm policy lapsed and that the health answers on it were wrong, so it would not have paid. Then help her see her options.
options.why: Honesty first. She cannot make a good decision without knowing where she stands.

options.t: Write a new application and answer "no" to the health questions that would cause a decline.
options.why: This is exactly what went wrong the first time. The policy will not pay, and you carry the risk.

options.t: Keep the Oxford policy in force. It is the only coverage she has today, and it should not lapse while a new one is set up.
options.why: Right and easy to forget, but secondary to being honest with her and writing the new plan truthfully.

options.t: Answer every question truthfully. Given her health, that points to a guaranteed issue plan with no health questions. Explain the waiting period (graded benefit) clearly and confirm the carrier will issue it.
options.why: A properly underwritten policy is the only kind that pays. It also matches what she is actually eligible for.

options.t: Write down what you found and report the earlier application to your agency compliance contact and the carrier.
options.why: The right thing to do, and it protects the next client. It comes after Rita is taken care of.

options.t: Tell her a guaranteed issue plan pays the full benefit from day one.
options.why: False. It has a graded benefit, and she needs to hear that before she buys.

groups.label: Likely objection
groups.hint: She says: "I thought I was covered, and I was not. Why should I trust you?"

options.t: Tell her it is the only option she has, so she should take it.
options.why: Pressure, and it repeats the very thing that hurt her.

options.t: "You have every right to ask. Let me show you in writing exactly what this plan pays and when, including the waiting period. I would rather you know it now than find out later. And I will help you find out what happened with the old policy."
options.why: Answers the trust question with transparency and proof rather than a promise.

options.t: Offer to see whether a lower premium fits her budget.
options.why: Helpful, but it does not address trust.

options.t: "I am different from the last agent. Just trust me."
options.why: Asks for trust without giving her a reason.

title: The First Knock
file: Suburban neighborhood, referred lead list plus cold doors
A warm first impression that earns 60 more seconds
story: You are about to knock on a door you have never visited. The first ten seconds decide whether they open it wider or close it.
prompt: Select every practice that earns a good first impression. Practices that pressure, block, or mislead cost points.

options.t: Keep talking past the point where they say they are not interested.
options.why: Disrespects a clear no and burns the door for good.

options.t: Say you are "just doing a survey" to get them talking, then pivot to the pitch.
options.why: A misleading opener. Honesty from the first sentence matters more than a clever hook.

options.t: Smile, make eye contact, and say your name and company before anything else.
options.why: A clear, honest opener builds trust in the first few seconds.

options.t: Hold your ID or a flyer where they can see it as the door opens.
options.why: Visible identification lowers suspicion immediately.

options.t: State the reason for the visit in one short sentence before asking for their time.
options.why: Respects their time and avoids the feeling of being ambushed.

options.t: Ask a genuine, low-pressure question that invites a yes or no, like whether they have a moment.
options.why: Gives them control over the interaction instead of assuming it.

options.t: Stand slightly to the side of the door, not blocking the peephole or the stoop.
options.why: Reduces how threatening the approach feels, before you've said a word.

options.t: Step inside if they hesitate at the door, since it is easier to talk that way.
options.why: Pressuring your way past a hesitation damages trust immediately and can be inappropriate.

title: Not Interested
file: Man in his 60s, opens the door briefly
"Not interested," starts easing the door shut
story: He says "not interested" almost before you finish your name, and starts easing the door shut.
prompt: What do you say in the two or three seconds you have left?

options.t: "Wait, you haven't even heard what I'm offering yet. It'll only take a minute!"
options.why: Pushes past a clear no, which usually feels like pressure rather than persistence.

options.t: "Everyone says that at first. Just give me two minutes and you'll see why."
options.why: A step better than arguing, but it still resists the no instead of respecting it.

options.t: "Totally understand — I'll leave a card in case that changes. Take care."
options.why: Respects the no immediately, leaves a low-pressure way back in, and protects the relationship for a future visit or referral.

options.t: Say "okay" and walk away without a word.
options.why: Respects the no, but leaves nothing behind for later.

title: Working the Block
file: A list of 20 addresses for a Saturday route
Working alone, reporting to a team leader that evening
story: Good door-knocking days follow the same shape, whether the first ten doors go well or not.
prompt: Put these five parts of a knocking session in the order you would run them.

steps.t: Debrief with your team leader that evening on what worked and what did not
steps.why: Closes the loop and improves the next route.

steps.t: Ask any interested prospect for a good time to follow up, or for someone else nearby worth visiting
steps.why: Turns one good knock into the next lead.

steps.t: Log the outcome of every door, answered or not, right after you leave it
steps.why: Memory fades fast across twenty doors; a log is what makes follow-up possible.

steps.t: Knock, introduce yourself, and state your reason for the visit
steps.why: The actual contact — the reason for the whole route.

steps.t: Review the route and whatever you know about each address before the first knock
steps.why: Preparing ahead avoids wasted time and awkward blank starts.

title: No Soliciting Sign
file: Posted "No Soliciting" sign by the door
This address mailed back a card asking for information
story: The house has a no-soliciting sign, but it is also on your list because the resident mailed back a card asking for information.
prompt: What do you do?

options.t: Knock anyway. The mailer response means they want to talk, and the sign is really meant for strangers selling door to door, not for someone they asked to hear from.
options.why: A posted sign generally means no door visits, even from someone who responded to a mailer through a different channel.

options.t: Skip the knock and reach out by phone or mail instead, since they invited contact but the sign asks you not to come to the door.
options.why: Respects the posted sign while still honoring the interest they expressed through a channel they did not restrict.

options.t: Knock, since the mailer counts as an invitation, so technically you are following up on a request and not really soliciting.
options.why: Rationalizing around a clearly posted rule.

options.t: Skip the address entirely and remove it from every list, since the sign tells you they do not want any contact at all.
options.why: Safe, but a warm mailer response is a real lead going to waste when another respectful contact method is easy.

title: The Skeptical Neighbor
file: She recently heard news about a scam targeting seniors
story: You have barely introduced yourself when she asks, flatly, if this is a scam.
prompt: Write what you would say next, in 2 to 4 sentences.

rubric.label: Takes the concern seriously, not defensively
rubric.tip: Meet the question with respect, not defensiveness — she has a real reason to ask.

rubric.label: Offers a concrete way to verify you
rubric.tip: Give her something she can actually check, not just your word.

rubric.label: States your name and company plainly
rubric.tip: Plain, upfront identification is the opposite of how a scam usually opens.

rubric.label: Gives her an easy out
rubric.tip: Show her the door is easy to close if she wants — pressure would confirm her suspicion.

rubric.label: Invites a small next step rather than a big ask
rubric.tip: Ask for something small first; a big ask right after 'is this a scam' rarely lands.

sample: That's a completely fair question, especially with what's been in the news. My name is on this card and I'm with Paragon — you're welcome to look up the company or ask for my license number before we talk further. I'm not asking for any money or account information today, just a couple of minutes to see if this is even something you'd want. If not, no pressure at all, and I'll leave you my card.

title: Setting the Appointment by Phone
file: Calling a lead who requested information by mail
Book a specific day and time for an in-home visit
story: A good appointment-setting call follows a simple shape, whether the lead is warm or lukewarm.
prompt: Put these five parts of the call in order.

steps.t: Ask a couple of quick qualifying questions, like who else is involved in the decision
steps.why: Makes sure the right people will actually be at the table.

steps.t: Introduce yourself and confirm you're speaking with the person who requested information
steps.why: Confirms you have the right person before anything else.

steps.t: Offer two specific times and let them choose one
steps.why: Two concrete options move faster to a decision than an open-ended 'when works for you.'

steps.t: Confirm the address, what to have ready, and repeat the day and time before hanging up
steps.why: Cuts down on no-shows and confusion on the day of.

steps.t: Remind them why they're hearing from you, tied to what they asked for
steps.why: Reduces the 'who is this' reaction and grounds the call.

title: The No-Show
file: No one answered the door; no call ahead
First missed appointment with this lead
story: You drove out for a 2 p.m. appointment and nobody answered. You're back in the car, phone in hand.
prompt: Write the voicemail or text you would leave, in 2 to 4 sentences.

rubric.label: Stays friendly, not accusatory
rubric.tip: A missed appointment isn't a confrontation — keep the tone light.

rubric.label: States plainly that you stopped by
rubric.tip: Simple, factual, no guilt attached.

rubric.label: Leaves the door open rather than writing them off
rubric.tip: One missed appointment is not the end of the lead.

rubric.label: Gives an easy way to reconnect
rubric.tip: Make the next step as easy as possible for them.

rubric.label: Suggests a specific next step rather than an open-ended one
rubric.tip: A concrete suggestion is easier to say yes to than 'whenever.'

sample: Hi, it's Sam from Paragon — I stopped by around 2 for our appointment but must have missed you, no worries at all. I hope everything's okay. I'd love to find another time this week if you're still interested — just call or text whenever works and we'll get something on the books.

title: Staying Compliant at the Table
file: In-home appointment, presenting a final expense plan
Written consent required before recording any conversation
story: You're at the kitchen table with a couple, ready to present. A few habits separate a clean, professional appointment from one that invites a complaint later.
prompt: Select every practice that belongs in a compliant, professional appointment.

options.t: Describe the benefit using only the terms that appear in the actual policy, not rounder or more generous language.
options.why: Prevents a mismatch between what was said and what was sold.

options.t: Rush past the health questions if they seem uncomfortable, and fill in your best guess.
options.why: Inaccurate answers can void the policy later and hurt the client badly.

options.t: Get clear consent before recording any part of the conversation, if you record at all.
options.why: Required in many states, and simply respectful regardless.

options.t: Skip the free-look explanation since most people never use it anyway.
options.why: Rarely used is not the same as not required — it's still a disclosure they're owed.

options.t: Tell them the rate is guaranteed never to change, even if the policy doesn't say that.
options.why: Misrepresents the product, whatever the intention.

options.t: Confirm the client understands the free-look period before they sign.
options.why: They're entitled to know they can cancel without penalty in that window.

options.t: Leave a copy of the application and any illustration with the client, not just a verbal summary.
options.why: Gives them a real record of exactly what they agreed to.

title: Reading the Room
file: Wife goes quiet and starts looking at her phone; husband keeps nodding
story: You're midway through your presentation. The husband keeps nodding along, but his wife has gone quiet and is now looking at her phone.
prompt: What's the best next move?

options.t: Keep presenting to the husband since he's clearly engaged and is likely the one who decides.
options.why: Ignoring a disengaged decision-maker risks losing the sale at the finish line.

options.t: Pause and gently bring her back in, like asking what questions are on her mind so far.
options.why: Re-engages the quieter decision-maker before momentum is lost, without calling her out.

options.t: Ask if now is a bad time and offer to reschedule the whole appointment for another day.
options.why: A safe fallback, but often unnecessary if a small check-in would re-engage her instead.

options.t: Speed up and get to the close quickly, before she checks out of the conversation completely.
options.why: Rushing past a disengaged spouse usually backfires right at signature time.

title: The Guarded Prospect
file: Woman, 68, answers questions with one word
story: Ten minutes into the visit, she's polite but closed off — short answers, no elaboration.
prompt: Which question is most likely to open her up?

options.t: "What is it you're worried might happen if something happened to you?"
options.why: Fear-first framing, before rapport is earned, tends to close a guarded person further.

options.t: "Tell me about your family — who's around, and who do you lean on?"
options.why: An easy, low-pressure topic most people open up about, and it surfaces who actually matters to the plan.

options.t: "What's your budget for something like this?"
options.why: Budget-first, before any need is established, and unlikely to loosen up someone already guarded.

options.t: "Do you already have life insurance?"
options.why: A fair fact-finding question, but closed-ended and less likely to open her up than a warmer topic.

title: Beneficiary Intentions
file: Retired couple, two children, one estranged
Discussing who the policy would be for
story: They've agreed they want coverage. Now you're figuring out who it's really for, and what they want it to do.
prompt: Select every question worth asking about beneficiaries and intent.

options.t: Is there anyone you'd specifically want to leave out, and is there anything I should know about how we set that up?
options.why: Surfaces a sensitive but important detail directly and respectfully.

options.t: Is there a charity or cause that matters enough to you to include?
options.why: Opens a real option many clients don't realize they have.

options.t: Would you want this to go to one person to divide, or split by percentage between people?
options.why: A concrete structural question that affects how the policy is written.

options.t: Wouldn't it just be easier to leave it all to whichever kid calls you the most?
options.why: Flippant, and not a genuine discovery question.

options.t: Who would you want to receive this, and are they able to handle the money responsibly?
options.why: Gets at both intent and practicality in one question.

options.t: How much money do your kids make?
options.why: Irrelevant and intrusive — it's not about their intent for the money.

title: Health and Budget Together
file: First fifteen minutes of a new appointment
story: A good discovery flow builds trust before it asks for numbers.
prompt: Put these five discovery topics in the order you would raise them.

steps.t: Ask about their wishes for arrangements and who would handle things
steps.why: Opens the real topic gently, before any numbers are on the table.

steps.t: Ask about monthly budget, now that the need and the options are clear
steps.why: Budget lands better once they understand what it's actually buying.

steps.t: Find out what coverage or savings already exists
steps.why: You need the current picture before you can find the actual gap.

steps.t: Build rapport and confirm what they're hoping to get out of the visit
steps.why: Sets the stage and lowers guard before anything sensitive comes up.

steps.t: Ask the health questions that affect what they qualify for
steps.why: Needed before anything can be accurately priced.

title: What They're Not Saying
file: Man, 66, says money is "tight but fine"
Hesitates, then changes the subject when asked about savings
story: He says money is "tight but fine" and quickly moves on when you ask about savings. Something in how he said it made you want to follow up, gently.
prompt: Write what you would say next, in 2 to 4 sentences.

rubric.label: Notices the hesitation without calling it out bluntly
rubric.tip: Name what you noticed gently, not as an accusation.

rubric.label: Normalizes the topic so it feels safe
rubric.tip: Money questions feel less exposing when framed as universal.

rubric.label: Reassures there's no judgment
rubric.tip: Say plainly that you're not evaluating him.

rubric.label: Keeps the question open, not a number demand
rubric.tip: Ask about the shape of it, not a hard figure.

rubric.label: Ties it back to finding the right fit, not qualifying him for a sale
rubric.tip: Frame the question as being in service of him, not your quota.

sample: I noticed that one shifted a little fast — no judgment at all, a lot of folks feel the same way about money questions. I'm not trying to pin down an exact number, just trying to understand what feels comfortable so whatever we land on actually fits. Can you tell me a bit more about what 'tight' looks like month to month?

title: Graded vs Level
file: Explaining benefit types to a new client
Some health conditions; might not qualify for full day-one coverage
story: A client asks you to explain the difference between the two plans on the table before deciding.
prompt: Select every statement that is true about graded vs. level benefit plans.

options.t: After the graded period ends, the policy pays the full face amount for any covered cause of death, the same as a level plan.
options.why: Correctly describes what happens once the graded period is over.

options.t: A level benefit plan pays the full face amount from day one, assuming the application is approved.
options.why: Correctly describes a level benefit plan.

options.t: Graded benefit plans exist so people who might not qualify for a level plan due to health can still get coverage.
options.why: Correctly states the purpose of the graded option.

options.t: Accidental death is excluded entirely during the graded period, with no benefit at all.
options.why: Usually incorrect — accidental death is typically still paid in full even during the graded period.

options.t: A graded benefit plan always costs less than a level plan for the same face amount.
options.why: Not reliably true — it's a health-based tradeoff, not simply a discount.

options.t: A graded benefit plan typically pays a reduced amount (often a return of premium plus interest) if death occurs from non-accidental causes in the first two to three years.
options.why: Correctly describes the standard graded structure.

title: Riders That Matter
file: Woman, 59, drives for a rideshare service most weekends
story: She wants to know if there's anything that would pay more if something happened to her while driving for work.
prompt: Which addition best fits what she's asking for?

options.t: An accidental death benefit rider, which pays an additional amount if death results from an accident.
options.why: Directly matches her stated concern about work-related driving risk.

options.t: A return of premium rider, which refunds all the premiums she has paid if she outlives the policy term, so the money is never wasted.
options.why: Doesn't address her stated concern about accidental death at all.

options.t: Raising the base face amount instead of adding a rider, so every kind of death pays more.
options.why: Would help generally, but doesn't specifically target the accidental scenario she described, and likely costs more for the same protection there.

options.t: A waiver of premium rider, which waives payments if she becomes disabled.
options.why: A useful rider in general, but not what she actually asked about.

title: Underwriting Class
file: Type 2 diabetes, diet-controlled, no complications. No heart, cancer, or stroke history. No tobacco.
Level benefit standard class, level benefit modified class, graded benefit
story: He answers the health questions clearly: diet-controlled diabetes with no complications, and nothing else.
prompt: Based only on what's known so far, which class does he most likely fit, pending formal underwriting?

options.t: Graded benefit, since any diabetes on the health questions usually means a waiting period before the full benefit pays.
options.why: Jumps to the most restrictive option without weighing severity — well-controlled diabetes with no complications often still qualifies for a level plan.

options.t: Level benefit, likely at a standard or modified rate depending on the carrier's specific guidelines for diet-controlled diabetes.
options.why: Matches the typical underwriting pattern, where well-managed, uncomplicated diabetes often still qualifies for day-one coverage, possibly at a different rate class.

options.t: Level benefit at the best possible rate, no different from someone with no health conditions at all, since his diabetes is controlled by diet alone.
options.why: Optimistic — diabetes usually affects rate class even when well-controlled.

options.t: It's impossible to say anything useful until the full application has been submitted and underwritten by the carrier.
options.why: The final word always comes from underwriting, but agents are expected to set honest expectations based on typical patterns.

title: Explain It Simply
file: Doesn't understand why one quote asks health questions and the other doesn't
story: She has two quotes in front of her and asks, "Why does this one ask about my health and the other one doesn't?"
prompt: Explain the difference in plain terms, in 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.label: Names both plan types in plain language
rubric.tip: Name the two paths clearly before explaining the tradeoff.

rubric.label: Explains the tradeoff (easier approval vs. cost or waiting period)
rubric.tip: Every 'easier' option trades something — say what.

rubric.label: Mentions the graded or waiting period on the no-questions option
rubric.tip: This is the detail clients are most often surprised by later if it's skipped.

rubric.label: Avoids jargon, or defines it immediately if used
rubric.tip: Translate any insurance term the moment you use it.

rubric.label: Connects it back to helping her choose, not just reciting facts
rubric.tip: End by applying it to her, not just the categories in general.

sample: Simply put, one plan asks a few health questions and, if you qualify, pays the full amount starting day one. The other skips the health questions entirely, which makes it easier to get approved, but in exchange it usually only pays a partial benefit if something happens in the first two or three years. Since your health sounds strong, the one with questions is likely the better fit and probably costs less for more coverage — let's go through the questions together and see.

title: The Assumptive Close
file: Client has agreed coverage makes sense, hasn't said yes to a specific plan yet
story: They've nodded along through the whole presentation and agreed they need something. Now it's time to move to paper.
prompt: Put these five moves in the order you would make them.

steps.t: Confirm next steps after signing, like when the policy will arrive
steps.why: Closes the loop and reduces any buyer's remorse.

steps.t: Summarize the plan they responded to best, in their own words
steps.why: Confirms you both agree on exactly what's being bought.

steps.t: State the next step as already happening, like 'let's get your application started'
steps.why: Assumes the yes rather than re-asking for permission.

steps.t: Hand them the pen or device and begin the first field together
steps.why: Momentum matters once the assumption has been made.

steps.t: Address any last hesitation as it comes up, calmly and specifically
steps.why: A late objection is normal and doesn't mean starting over.

title: Closing With Both Spouses
file: Husband ready to sign, wife hasn't said much
story: He's ready to go. She's been quieter through the whole visit and hasn't clearly said yes or no.
prompt: Select every practice that respects both decision-makers at the close.

options.t: Address any concern she raises as seriously as his enthusiasm.
options.why: Treats both perspectives as equally valid.

options.t: Make sure both names are said and both are looking at the same numbers before asking for the decision.
options.why: Keeps both of them equally informed at the moment of decision.

options.t: Ask her directly, by name, how she's feeling about it before moving to paperwork.
options.why: Gives the quieter decision-maker a real, direct opening.

options.t: Direct all your eye contact and questions to him since he's the one talking.
options.why: Sidelines the quieter decision-maker at the exact moment she matters most.

options.t: Move forward with the application since one spouse already said yes.
options.why: Risks a decision that doesn't hold, or a spouse who feels steamrolled.

options.t: Confirm both of them, not just him, understand what happens next.
options.why: Closes the loop for both decision-makers, not just the more vocal one.

title: The Callback Close
file: She said "let me think about it" and asked for a callback in a week
story: A week ago she asked for time to think. You're calling back exactly when you said you would.
prompt: How do you open the callback?

options.t: "Hi, it's back from last week — have you had a chance to think it over? What questions came up?"
options.why: Follows through as promised, opens with a real question rather than a pitch, and invites whatever is actually on her mind.

options.t: "Hi, just calling to see if you're ready to sign now. I can have the paperwork over today."
options.why: Skips past whatever she was actually thinking about and pushes straight to close.

options.t: "Hi, I wanted to give you a heads-up that rates are going up soon, so now's really the best time to lock in your price before they change."
options.why: Manufactured urgency instead of following up on her actual concern.

options.t: "Hi, just checking in. No pressure at all, give me a call whenever you're ready to talk."
options.why: Respectful, but passive — she asked for a specific callback and a real conversation, not just a soft touch.

title: Building to Yes
file: Doesn't want to be a burden on her sister, her only close family
Says she'll "probably get around to it eventually"
story: Diane has been engaged through the whole visit and agrees the numbers make sense. When you ask if she's ready to move forward, she says, "I'll probably get around to it eventually."
prompt: Build your close. Choose the strongest logical reasons, the strongest emotional reasons, and the best response to her hesitation.

groups.label: Logical reasons
groups.hint: Pick the two facts that make the strongest case on paper.

options.t: She already agrees the plan fits — the only thing left to decide is timing, not whether.
options.why: Names exactly where she stands, precisely.

options.t: Most people who say 'eventually' mean 'never.'
options.why: Presumptuous and vaguely insulting.

options.t: "Eventually" has no guaranteed date, and health or price can change before then.
options.why: Names the real risk in waiting, without pressure.

options.t: The industry could raise rates next year.
options.why: True in general, but not tied to her specific situation.

options.t: She should compare three more quotes before deciding.
options.why: Undermines your own recommendation and stalls rather than closes.

options.t: Her sister is getting older too, so timing matters for both of them.
options.why: Relevant secondary point, true but not the sharpest of the set.

groups.label: Emotional reasons
groups.hint: Pick the two that connect to what she actually said she wants.

options.t: Bring up that her late plans would disappoint someone if she waits.
options.why: A guilt tactic with no basis in anything she said.

options.t: Remind her this is exactly the situation she's worried about, still fresh in her mind.
options.why: Reasonable, but less sharp than the top two and risks feeling repetitive.

options.t: Getting this settled now means her sister never has to wonder or worry later.
options.why: Ties directly to the person she cares about.

options.t: She'll feel relieved once it's handled.
options.why: True but generic, secondary to the two specific ones.

options.t: She said she doesn't want to be a burden — this plan is the difference between that fear and the reality.
options.why: Reflects her own words back to her.

options.t: Point out how alone she must feel now.
options.why: Not tied to the plan, and dwells on something she didn't raise.

groups.label: Likely objection
groups.hint: She says: "I'll probably get around to it eventually."

options.t: "If you don't do it now, you might not qualify later."
options.why: Fear-based pressure not tied to anything she's actually said.

options.t: "Of course, no rush — call me whenever you're ready."
options.why: Fully yields to the stall.

options.t: "You said this fits and protects your sister — the only thing 'eventually' changes is whether that's true today or later. Why not make it true today?"
options.why: Reflects her own words back and asks a direct, respectful question.

options.t: "Okay, I'll follow up in a month."
options.why: Passive — doesn't attempt to address the stall right now at all.

title: What You Must Disclose
file: Client asks, "Is there anything I should know before I sign?"
story: Right before signing, she asks if there's anything she should know.
prompt: What's the most complete, honest answer?

options.t: "Just that you're covered from the day it's approved. That's really all that matters for now."
options.why: Brushes past a direct question that deserves a real answer.

options.t: "Yes — the free-look period, when premiums are due, anything excluded, and who to call with questions."
options.why: Covers the key things a client is entitled to know before signing, honestly and completely.

options.t: "Nothing you need to worry about. I've handled all the details, so you can just sign right here."
options.why: Dismisses a legitimate question and withholds information she's entitled to.

options.t: "Mainly the free-look period, which gives you a window after the policy arrives to cancel for a full refund if you change your mind."
options.why: Correct but incomplete — a few other things are worth naming too.

title: The Replacement Notice
file: Client is replacing an existing policy with a new one
story: She's decided to replace her old policy with the new one you've presented. Replacing a policy comes with extra steps most sales don't need.
prompt: Put these five replacement steps in the order they belong.

steps.t: Confirm with her that the old policy is cancelled and she has the new policy in hand
steps.why: Closes the loop so nothing is left in a gray area.

steps.t: Complete the required replacement notice or comparison form
steps.why: The documented step that must happen before the old policy is touched.

steps.t: Wait for the new policy to be approved and in force before the old one is cancelled
steps.why: Prevents a gap where she would have no coverage at all.

steps.t: Confirm she understands this is a replacement, not an addition, and why
steps.why: She should clearly understand what's happening before anything else.

steps.t: Submit the new application along with the replacement paperwork
steps.why: The new coverage process, done properly and in the right order.

title: Red Flags
file: A recent acquaintance has been present at the last two appointments and does most of the talking
story: The same acquaintance has been at her last two appointments, answering questions before she can, and pushing for a larger policy than she originally asked for.
prompt: Select every sign here worth pausing on and raising with your team leader or compliance contact.

options.t: She lives alone.
options.why: Also not itself a red flag; it's context, not a warning sign on its own.

options.t: She seems to defer to this person rather than answering in her own words.
options.why: A sign her own voice may not be driving the decision.

options.t: Someone outside her immediate family is directing the conversation and answering for her.
options.why: A real pattern worth noting, regardless of the acquaintance's intentions.

options.t: The beneficiary designation is being suggested by the acquaintance, not by her.
options.why: Directly affects who benefits, and should come from the client.

options.t: The push is for a larger policy than she originally said she wanted.
options.why: A shift in scope that didn't come from the client herself.

options.t: She is 82 years old.
options.why: Age alone is not a red flag — the behavior around her is what matters.

title: The Widow's Sister
file: One sister, also older, lives two states away
Just paid for her husband's funeral on a credit card, still paying it off
story: Pauline mentions, almost in passing, that she put her husband's funeral on a credit card and is still paying it down eight months later. She says, "I don't want to be a bill for anyone."
prompt: Build your angle: pick the strongest logical reasons, emotional reasons, and best response to her likely hesitation.

groups.label: Logical reasons
groups.hint: Pick the two facts from her situation that make the strongest case on paper.

options.t: She just lived through exactly the problem this plan solves, in her own recent experience.
options.why: Directly ties the recommendation to something she personally just went through.

options.t: She should have planned this years ago.
options.why: Unhelpful hindsight, not persuasive in the moment.

options.t: Final costs are rising every year industry-wide.
options.why: True in general, but not specific to her situation.

options.t: She has no children, so no one else will step up.
options.why: Presumptuous, and not something she has said.

options.t: Paying off a funeral on a credit card adds interest on top of the original cost — a plan avoids that entirely for whoever handles hers.
options.why: A concrete financial fact tied to her exact situation.

options.t: Her sister is older too and lives far away, so she can't easily be the one to handle logistics.
options.why: Relevant secondary point, true but not the sharpest of the set.

groups.label: Emotional reasons
groups.hint: Pick the two that connect to what she actually said.

options.t: Point out how alone she must feel now.
options.why: Not tied to the plan, and dwells on grief unnecessarily.

options.t: Bring up that her late husband would be disappointed she hasn't handled this yet.
options.why: A guilt tactic that invokes her late spouse.

options.t: Her sister, not a stranger, would be the one figuring this out — this spares the person she loves most from the same experience she just had.
options.why: Names exactly who benefits and why it matters to her.

options.t: She said she doesn't want to be a bill for anyone — this plan is the difference between that fear and the reality.
options.why: Reflects her own words directly back to her.

options.t: Remind her this is exactly what just happened to her, still fresh.
options.why: Reasonable, but risks feeling repetitive after the logical group already used this angle.

options.t: She'll feel relieved once it's handled.
options.why: True but generic, secondary to the two specific ones.

groups.label: Likely objection
groups.hint: She hesitates: "I need to think about the cost, money's tight right now after everything."

options.t: "Of course — take all the time you need."
options.why: Fully yields to the stall.

options.t: "This is cheaper than what you just went through, so it's really a no-brainer."
options.why: Dismissive framing of a real budget concern.

options.t: "I hear that, and it's exactly why a small monthly plan makes more sense than another bill all at once, like what just happened. What amount would feel manageable?"
options.why: Acknowledges the real constraint and reframes toward a workable number rather than a yes or no.

options.t: "I can come back next month once things settle."
options.why: Passive — doesn't attempt to solve the actual concern raised.

title: The Caregiver's Neighbor
file: A longtime neighbor, Dot, checks on him daily and drives him to appointments
One son, lives across the country, rarely visits
Wants to leave something for Dot, but is unsure if that's "allowed"
story: Harold says, quietly, "Dot's done more for me the last two years than my own son. I'd like to leave her something, but I don't know if you can even do that."
prompt: Build your angle: pick the strongest logical reasons, emotional reasons, and best response to his hesitation.

groups.label: Logical reasons
groups.hint: Pick the two facts that make the strongest case on paper.

options.t: A beneficiary can be anyone he names — it doesn't have to be a blood relative.
options.why: Directly answers the question he actually asked.

options.t: His son, being far away, may not be positioned to handle arrangements quickly anyway.
options.why: Relevant secondary point, true but less central than the top two.

options.t: Naming Dot directly avoids the delay and cost of probate that leaving it in a will might create.
options.why: A concrete practical advantage of a named beneficiary over a will.

options.t: A life insurance payout goes directly to the named beneficiary, outside the estate process.
options.why: True and relevant, close behind the top two but more technical than personally persuasive.

options.t: He should leave everything to his son regardless, since that's traditional.
options.why: Overrides his stated wish without any real basis.

options.t: Dot is younger and more likely to outlive him than his son is to visit.
options.why: An odd, irrelevant line of reasoning.

groups.label: Emotional reasons
groups.hint: Pick the two that connect to what he actually said.

options.t: He can honor, in a concrete way, the person who has actually shown up for him.
options.why: Directly reflects his own stated reasoning.

options.t: Point out his son should feel guilty for not visiting.
options.why: Invites guilt and conflict that isn't his concern.

options.t: This is his last chance to make it right.
options.why: Unnecessarily dramatic and pressuring.

options.t: He'll feel lighter knowing it's settled and reflects what he actually wants.
options.why: True but generic.

options.t: This removes any doubt about whether it's 'allowed' — it's entirely his choice to make.
options.why: Addresses his exact hesitation.

options.t: Dot deserves it more than his son does.
