options.why: Not his words, and puts you in the middle of a comparison he didn't ask for.

groups.label: Likely objection
groups.hint: He hesitates: "I just don't want it to seem strange to people."

options.t: "You're right, maybe stick with your son to keep it simple."
options.why: Talks him out of his own stated wish.

options.t: "I can't really weigh in on that, it's between you and your family."
options.why: Unhelpfully neutral, avoiding support on a legitimate concern he raised with you directly.

options.t: "It's your decision to make, and it's a common one — plenty of people name someone who's shown up for them, not just family."
options.why: Normalizes his choice and affirms it's his to make, without pressure.

options.t: "Don't worry about what people think."
options.why: Dismissive, and doesn't really address his specific worry.

title: The Quiet Spouse
file: Two grown sons. June's sister passed away four months ago
Social Security and a small pension
Early in the conversation, before any plans or prices
story: When you mention that most families you meet are thinking about funeral costs, June goes quiet. She looks down at the table and starts folding her napkin. Harold keeps talking about his golf league.
prompt: What do you do right now, before moving on?

options.t: Tell her kindly that everyone gets emotional about this topic and that it is completely normal, then gently move on to the next page so she does not feel put on the spot.
options.why: Kind on the surface, but it tells her how to feel instead of asking. It closes the door you should be opening.

options.t: Turn to Harold and ask more about his golf league to lighten the mood, then come back to the funeral topic once June seems more comfortable.
options.why: Friendly, but it walks away from the person who just signaled something important.

options.t: Pause and say gently, "June, it looked like that brought something up for you. Has your family been through a funeral recently?" Then listen before you go any further.
options.why: Naming what you noticed, gently, lets her share the loss now. Her experience becomes a reason for the plan instead of an unspoken feeling that turns into "we need to think about it" at the close.

options.t: Keep going so you do not lose momentum, and make a note to check in with June at the close, once the numbers are in front of both of them.
options.why: Momentum is not worth it. Whatever she is feeling does not go away. It usually comes back as hesitation right when you ask for the decision.

title: Burned Before
file: Bought a policy three years ago from another agent. She changed banks, the draft failed, the policy lapsed and no one called her
$1,650 a month Social Security, paid on the third Wednesday
What she said at the door
"I tried this once. I paid for a year and got nothing. I am not doing that again."
story: Delores lets you in, but she sits back with her purse on her lap. She says she only agreed to talk because her neighbor vouched for you.
prompt: Plan how you will handle her past experience before you ever present a plan. Choose what to acknowledge, what to build into the sit, and the objection you are heading off.

groups.label: Acknowledge it first
groups.hint: Pick the two things to do before you present anything.

options.t: Tell her the other agent was probably a crook.
options.why: You do not know the full story, and bashing another agent makes you look like one more salesperson.

options.t: Let her know you will leave your direct number and check in after the policy is issued.
options.why: Good follow-through, but it lands better once you know what went wrong.

options.t: Ask what happened with that policy, and let her tell the whole story before you present anything.
options.why: The details tell you exactly which worry you need to answer. Here, it was a missed draft that nobody told her about.

options.t: Tell her you are sorry that happened, and that it is a fair reason to be careful.
options.why: Validating her caution earns you the right to keep going.

options.t: Promise that nothing like that could ever happen with your company.
options.why: A promise you cannot keep. Overpromising is how the next broken trust starts.

options.t: Skip it. Bringing up bad memories will only hurt the mood.
options.why: The memory is already in the room. Ignoring it leaves it to surface at the close.

groups.label: Build it into the sit
groups.hint: Pick the two steps that directly answer what went wrong last time.

options.t: Explain the grace period: what happens if a payment is missed and how she would be notified.
options.why: Answers the exact thing that hurt her last time, before she has to ask.

options.t: Tell her not to worry about payments, since policies rarely lapse.
options.why: Hers did. Dismissing it tells her you were not listening.

options.t: Where the carrier offers it, add a trusted family member to receive a notice if a payment is ever missed.
options.why: A strong extra safeguard, but the first two fix the root cause.

options.t: Set the draft date to line up with the day her Social Security arrives.
options.why: Many lapses start with a draft date that does not match when money comes in.

options.t: Move quickly through the application so she does not have time to worry.
options.why: Rushing someone who has been burned confirms her fear.

groups.label: The objection you are heading off
groups.hint: If none of this came up until the close, what would she most likely say?

options.t: "I do not need life insurance."
options.why: She tried to buy a policy before. Need is not the issue.

options.t: "I have been through this before. I am not signing anything today."
options.why: Right. Her past experience, left unaddressed, is exactly what stops the close.

options.t: "It is too expensive."
options.why: Possible, but nothing she said points to price.

options.t: "I need to talk to my kids first."
options.why: Not what her story is signaling.

title: Signs Around the Kitchen
file: Rosa mentions their pharmacy copays went up this year. Their son moved back in after losing his job
story: Walt says, "Everything costs more than it used to." Rosa nods and adds that they have been "juggling a few things" since their son moved home.
prompt: Select every move that deals with budget now, so it does not turn into "we cannot afford it" at the close. Moves that pressure or embarrass them cost points.

options.t: Point out the past-due notice you saw on the counter.
options.why: Embarrassing. Let them share what they choose to share.

options.t: Size the coverage to the funeral and final bills they described, not to the largest plan available.
options.why: A plan built around their stated need is easier to say yes to and to keep paying.

options.t: Show the biggest plan first so there is room to come down.
options.why: After they told you money is tight, anchoring high feels like pressure.

options.t: Acknowledge what you heard: "It sounds like this year has been tight, with the copays going up and your son at home."
options.why: Showing you heard it makes it safe for them to be honest about money.

options.t: Let them know the coverage amount can be adjusted to fit the budget they give you.
options.why: Takes away the fear that saying their real number means walking away with nothing.

options.t: Keep money out of the conversation until the very end so the mood stays positive.
options.why: Waiting guarantees that the budget becomes the objection.

options.t: Before showing any numbers, ask: "What would feel comfortable each month without taking from groceries or medicine?"
options.why: Agreeing on a budget first means the plan you show already fits.

title: Who Else Decides?
file: Daughter Karen, 52, lives ten minutes away
story: Ruth is warm and engaged. She says she wants to make sure Karen is not stuck with the funeral bill, and mentions in passing that Karen handles her checkbook.
prompt: What is the best move right now?

options.t: Suggest finishing the application today before Karen gets involved, so the decision stays simple and Ruth does not feel second-guessed.
options.why: Steering a senior away from the family member who manages her money is a red flag. It also leads to cancellations once Karen finds out.

options.t: Ask Ruth whether she is still allowed to make her own financial decisions, or whether Karen needs to sign everything for her now.
options.why: Condescending. It questions her dignity instead of including her family.

options.t: Note it on your sheet, keep going with discovery, and plan to handle Karen if Ruth brings her up again at the close, since Ruth is the one being insured.
options.why: You already know who helps decide. Waiting almost guarantees the stall.

options.t: Ask now: "Since Karen helps with your bills, would you like her to be part of this? We can call her now, or set a time when she can join us."
options.why: Bringing the person who helps with money in early prevents "I need to talk to my daughter" at the close, and it protects Ruth by keeping her family informed.

title: Set It Up Early
file: Reach the close with no surprises left
"Let us think about it," "I need to talk to my kids," "It costs too much"
story: Most objections at the close are things the client was already thinking in the first ten minutes. The order of your conversation decides whether they come out early, when you can address them, or late, when they stop the sale.
prompt: Put these steps in the order that brings concerns out early and keeps the close free of surprises.

steps.t: Set expectations: explain what you will cover, and agree that at the end they can make a clear yes or no decision
steps.why: Agreeing up front that a decision is expected prevents "we will think about it" later.

steps.t: Confirm who else should be part of the decision, and agree on a comfortable monthly budget
steps.why: Handles the two most common stalls, the absent family member and the price, before any numbers appear.

steps.t: Ask about past experiences with insurance and funerals, and what worries them, and acknowledge each one
steps.why: This is where the future objections live. Acknowledged now, they become reasons instead of barriers.

steps.t: Ask for the decision
steps.why: By now the usual objections have already been answered.

steps.t: Build rapport and learn a little about their life and family
steps.why: People share concerns with someone they are comfortable with.

steps.t: Present the plan that fits, tying each part back to what they told you
steps.why: When the plan is built from their words, there is little left to object to.

title: The Skeptic's Tell
file: Arms crossed, sitting back from the table
"I have heard these companies always find a reason not to pay."
The first few minutes of the sit
story: Vernon says it half joking, but he is watching you closely to see how you react.
prompt: How do you handle it?

options.t: Tell him that is a great question, and that you will cover exactly how claims work at the end of the presentation if he still has concerns.
options.why: Postponing it guarantees it comes back as the objection.

options.t: Say, "That is a fair concern, and I would rather cover it now than at the end." Then explain how claims are paid, the contestable period, and why honest health answers make a claim pay.
options.why: Addresses the trust issue at the moment he raises it. The honest explanation is itself the reassurance, and it keeps the concern from resurfacing at the close.

options.t: Tell him with a smile that it is a common myth, that claims get paid every day, and move on to your presentation so the mood stays light.
options.why: Dismissing it leaves his doubt in place for the whole sit.

options.t: Tell him your company has the best claims record in the industry, so he has nothing to worry about, and offer to show him the brochure with its ratings and testimonials from other families.
options.why: An unverifiable claim sounds like a sales line, which is exactly what he expects.

title: Coverage Mentioned in Passing
file: Earl, 68, retiring from the pipefitters next year
"I think I have something through the union."
story: Earl mentions the union coverage while talking about something else and moves right on. He does not seem sure how much it is or how long it lasts.
prompt: Select every question worth asking now, so "I already have coverage" does not come up at the close. Moves that dismiss or undermine his coverage cost points.

options.t: "Does it stay with you after you retire, or does it end when you leave the union or reach a certain age?"
options.why: Group coverage often ends or shrinks at retirement. That is the gap that matters here.

options.t: Skip it, since talking about it will only lower the amount he needs.
options.why: Ignoring it means it becomes the objection, and it puts the sale ahead of the client.

options.t: "Who is listed as the beneficiary, and does your family know about it?"
options.why: Uncovers outdated beneficiaries and shows you care about the whole picture.

options.t: "Would what it pays cover the funeral you would want, plus any final bills?"
options.why: Turns his existing coverage into a clear view of what is covered and what is not.

options.t: Tell him union policies are usually not worth much.
options.why: You have not seen it, and running it down sounds self-serving.

options.t: "Do you know how much it pays? Do you have the paperwork handy?"
options.why: You cannot plan around coverage you have not seen.

options.t: Suggest he cancel it so there is no confusion.
options.why: Never suggest cancelling coverage, and never before new coverage is in force. It may be valuable.

title: The Pause Before Answering
file: On the health questions, she hesitates at "treated for COPD" and glances at her husband
A wrong answer can lead to a declined claim, and a surprise decline later destroys trust
story: Marlene says, "Well... I use an inhaler sometimes," then trails off and looks at you to see what happens next.
prompt: What is the best response?

options.t: Say, "Take your time. Honest answers are what make the claim pay. A diagnosis does not mean you cannot get covered. It just helps me find the right company for you."
options.why: Many carriers accept COPD, depending on details like steroid inhalers and recent hospital stays. Reassuring her that honesty helps, not hurts, gets accurate answers and prevents a declined claim or a surprise decline later.

options.t: Warn her gently that COPD will probably disqualify her at most companies, so she is prepared if the application comes back declined and is not disappointed or embarrassed later.
options.why: Not accurate. Several carriers accept COPD, and scaring her makes honest answers less likely.

options.t: Ask her husband to answer the rest of the health questions instead, since he may remember her medical history more clearly.
options.why: She is the insured. Her answers need to be her own.

options.t: Mark "no," since she only uses the inhaler sometimes and never actually said a doctor diagnosed or treated her for COPD.
options.why: That is misrepresentation. It can void the policy at claim time, which is the worst outcome for her family.

title: The Funeral She Already Paid For
file: A son and a daughter, both with young kids
"When my husband died I had to put $9,000 on a credit card. I am still paying it off."
story: Gloria says it quietly, almost as an aside, then starts to change the subject.
prompt: Write what you would say right after she tells you this, in 2 to 5 sentences. Acknowledge it and connect it to what she wants for her kids, without pressure.

rubric.label: Acknowledges what she went through
rubric.tip: Start with the person, not the plan.

rubric.label: Reflects back her specific experience
rubric.tip: Using her own details shows you listened.

rubric.label: Connects it to what she wants for her children
rubric.tip: Her experience is the reason. Tie it to the people she is protecting.

rubric.label: Links to the plan without pressure
rubric.tip: Show how it connects, but do not push.

rubric.label: Invites her to keep talking
rubric.tip: A question keeps her talking and brings out anything else on her mind.

sample: I am so sorry. That is a lot to carry, still paying off that credit card two years later. It sounds like you would not want your son and daughter to go through the same thing. Can I ask, would it mean a lot to you to have the funeral already taken care of, so they can focus on each other instead of the bill?

title: Two Spouses, Two Worries
file: "We are fine. We do not need anything."
Paid most of her mother's funeral last year. She is the one who called you
Social Security plus Frank's small pension
story: Linda leans in when you talk about final expenses. Frank checks his phone and says they are fine. Linda goes quiet when he says it.
prompt: Plan how you will bring both of them along before you present. Choose what to pick up on, how to acknowledge both of them, and the objection you are preventing.

groups.label: What to pick up on
groups.hint: Pick the two things that matter most for getting both of them on board.

options.t: Frank's "we are fine" may be about not wanting to feel he has not provided, rather than about need.
options.why: Reading what is behind his words lets you respect him instead of arguing with him.

options.t: Frank is the decision-maker, so focus your attention on him.
options.why: Ignoring Linda loses the person who already sees the need.

options.t: Linda seems emotional, so she will be easier to close.
options.why: Treating her feelings as leverage is manipulation.

options.t: Linda's experience paying for her mother's funeral.
options.why: Her firsthand experience is the real reason you are there.

options.t: They drive a newer car.
options.why: Not relevant to what is happening at this table.

options.t: They live on a fixed income.
options.why: Important for the budget, but secondary to getting them aligned.

groups.label: How to acknowledge both
groups.hint: Pick the two moves that bring both spouses into the conversation.

options.t: Speak mostly to Linda, since she already sees the need.
options.why: Frank will stall the decision if he feels left out.

options.t: Ask Frank what "fine" looks like if something happened tomorrow: who would handle the costs, and how?
options.why: A respectful question lets him see the gap himself.

options.t: Show them a chart of average funeral costs.
options.why: Useful context, but facts alone do not align two people.

options.t: Tell Frank he is not thinking about Linda.
options.why: Blaming him guarantees he digs in.

options.t: Invite Linda to share what happened with her mother, then ask Frank how that time was for them as a couple.
options.why: Brings Linda's experience into the open and lets Frank connect to it.

groups.label: The objection you are preventing
groups.hint: If they reach the close still split, what will you most likely hear?

options.t: "We cannot qualify."
options.why: Nothing points to a health concern.

options.t: "Let us talk it over and get back to you."
options.why: Right. Two spouses who are not aligned almost always stall to talk privately.

options.t: "The monthly cost is too high."
options.why: Possible later, but the split between them is the bigger risk.

options.t: "We already have coverage."
options.why: Nothing they said suggests existing coverage.

title: The TV Ad
file: "I keep seeing that ad on TV. It is only $9.95 a month and no health questions."
Early in the sit, before any plans
story: Bernice brings it up while you are still getting to know her. She seems to think it is the obvious choice.
prompt: What is the best way to handle it?

options.t: Tell her those TV ads are basically scams that never pay out, so she is much better off working with a licensed agent.
options.why: They are real products. Calling them scams costs you credibility.

options.t: Say nothing about it for now. If you bring up the TV ad yourself, she will just start comparing prices instead of listening.
options.why: She is already comparing. Staying quiet leaves the TV price as her benchmark.

options.t: Acknowledge it now: "Those ads are everywhere. Can I show you what that $9.95 buys at your age and how it pays out, next to what we find for you, so you can compare?"
options.why: Those plans often buy a small amount of coverage that depends on age, usually with a waiting period before the full benefit pays. An honest side-by-side now keeps it from becoming "I can get it cheaper on TV" at the close.

options.t: Wait until she brings it up again at the close, then handle it with a side-by-side comparison of the two plans, so the TV price does not distract her during your presentation.
options.why: You would handle it eventually, but at the close it arrives as an objection instead of a comparison.

title: When They Share Something Hard
file: Midway through discovery, a client tells you about a painful experience, such as a loss, a denied claim, or a bill that fell on family
How you respond decides whether it becomes a reason to act or a reason to stall
story: The moment a client shares something personal is one of the most important in the sit. Handled well, it builds trust and gives the plan its purpose. Rushed, it becomes a hidden objection.
prompt: Put these steps in the order you would use them.

steps.t: Ask a follow-up question to understand what mattered most to them
steps.why: The details tell you what the plan needs to solve.

steps.t: Later, when presenting, connect the plan back to that experience in their own words
steps.why: Their story becomes the reason for the plan, which leaves little to object to at the close.

steps.t: Acknowledge the feeling in your own words
steps.why: Naming it tells them they were heard.

steps.t: Stop what you are doing and give them your full attention
steps.why: Setting down the paperwork shows the story matters more than the sale.

steps.t: Summarize what you heard, and check that you got it right
steps.why: Confirming prevents you from building the plan on a wrong assumption.

title: The Insulin Question
file: Type 2 diabetes diagnosed at 58, now on insulin. No complications
story: Dale says, "My last guy told me insulin means I can only get one of those no-questions plans."
prompt: Based on our underwriting guide, which statement is accurate?

options.t: AIG SIWL would give him a level plan, because his diabetes has no complications and he was diagnosed well after age 45.
options.why: AIG goes by A1C. An A1C of 8.7 to 9.9 is graded, and his is 9.2.

options.t: Mutual of Omaha Living Promise accepts insulin-treated diabetes diagnosed after 45, and Royal Neighbors accepts insulin with no complications. He has full-benefit options.
options.why: Correct. Diagnosed at 58 on insulin with no complications, he fits both. Knowing this beats settling for a guaranteed issue plan.

options.t: His last agent was right. Any diabetes treated with insulin means a guaranteed issue plan with a two-year waiting period is his only option, no matter when he was diagnosed.
options.why: Wrong, and it would cost him two years of reduced coverage he does not need.

options.t: Mutual of Omaha Term Life Express declines anyone on insulin, so his best level options are with other carriers.
options.why: Not per our guide. Term Life Express approves insulin when diagnosed over 45. It declines diagnosis under 45.

title: Oxygen in the Corner
file: COPD. Uses supplemental oxygen most afternoons
An oxygen concentrator next to her recliner
story: Irene sees you glance at the concentrator and says, "Oh, I only use that sometimes."
prompt: Select every statement that is accurate per our guide. Wrong or dishonest moves cost points.

options.t: Royal Neighbors lists any oxygen use under guaranteed issue.
options.why: Correct. That keeps a door open, with a waiting period she needs to understand.

options.t: Mutual of Omaha Living Promise, Americo and Foresters will not issue while she currently uses oxygen.
options.why: Correct. All three list current oxygen use as a decline.

options.t: AIG SIWL accepts oxygen use for COPD.
options.why: AIG declines oxygen use except for sleep apnea.

options.t: Ask when she last used it and why. Oxygen with a CPAP for sleep apnea is treated differently from oxygen for COPD.
options.why: CVS and AIG both carve out CPAP for sleep apnea, so the reason matters.

options.t: Tell her no company will cover her.
options.why: False. Our guide shows graded and guaranteed issue options.

options.t: Transamerica FE Express lists supplemental oxygen within the last 12 months as graded.
options.why: Correct. Another real option to compare.

options.t: Leave the oxygen off, since she only uses it sometimes.
options.why: Misrepresentation. It can void the policy at claim time.

title: Fourteen Months After the Heart Attack
file: Heart attack 14 months ago. A stent was placed at the same time. Doing well since
story: Ray assumes he will have to "wait out" the heart attack before anyone will give him a real policy.
prompt: Which recommendation is the best fit per our guide?

options.t: AIG SIWL, which gives a non-smoker a level plan after a heart attack in the last 24 months, as long as it was more than 6 months ago, so he qualifies for their full benefit.
options.why: True for the heart attack, but AIG grades a stent in the last 24 months. His stent makes it graded.

options.t: Mutual of Omaha Living Promise with a full benefit from day one, since his heart attack was more than a year ago.
options.why: Living Promise grades a heart attack or stent within 2 years.

options.t: Wait until the two-year mark before applying anywhere, since every carrier treats a heart attack in the last 2 years as graded.
options.why: He would go uncovered for 10 months for no reason. Level options exist today.

options.t: Americo, which accepts a heart attack after one year and accepts stents, or CVS, which lists a heart attack 1 to 2 years ago as a standard level plan. Both are level.
options.why: Correct. At 14 months he is past Americo's one-year mark and in CVS's 1 to 2 year window, so he can have level coverage now.

title: Paying From an Online Bank
file: Social Security is deposited to an online-only bank account. She also has a prepaid debit card
story: Tanya is ready to go and asks, "Can you just take it off my card?"
prompt: Select every statement that is accurate per our guide. Moves that risk a failed draft or a lapse cost points.

options.t: Mutual of Omaha can take her card.
options.why: Our guide lists Mutual of Omaha as no cards.

options.t: Have her open a new bank account sometime after the policy is issued.
options.why: If the first draft fails, the policy can lapse before she ever gets to it.

options.t: Americo, Foresters and LBL will not draft from cards or online-only banks.
options.why: Correct, and it rules them out for her current setup.

options.t: Ask how and where she gets her Social Security before choosing a carrier, so the plan can actually be drafted.
options.why: Failed drafts are one of the most common reasons policies lapse.

options.t: Transamerica and AIG SIWL accept all payment methods on our guide.
options.why: Correct. They can work with how she actually gets paid.

options.t: Any carrier works as long as she has a routing number.
options.why: Several carriers refuse online-only banks even with a routing number.

title: Three Years Past Treatment
file: Breast cancer. Last treatment 3 years ago. No recurrence, did not spread
story: Carol says, "I figured cancer means I would be stuck with a waiting period."
prompt: Which statement is accurate per our guide?

options.t: Americo accepts cancer more than 2 years out, and Transamerica Immediate Solution lists cancer over 2 years as Standard. She can have a full benefit now.
options.why: Correct. Three years out with no recurrence or spread fits both.

options.t: AIG SIWL at a level benefit, since it only declines stage III or IV cancers and cancers that have come back.
options.why: AIG grades cancer diagnosed or treated within the last 48 months.

options.t: She is right. Any cancer treated in the last 4 or 5 years means guaranteed issue with a two-year waiting period is her only option, even when it did not spread.
options.why: Wrong. Settling for a waiting period she does not need costs her family.

options.t: Mutual of Omaha Living Promise with a full benefit from day one, since her cancer did not spread or come back.
options.why: Living Promise grades cancer within 4 years.

title: Stroke and Diabetes
file: One stroke 18 months ago, fully recovered. Type 2 diabetes, pills only
story: Gordon mentions both conditions in the same breath and asks what that means for him.
prompt: Select every statement that is accurate per our guide.

options.t: Americo accepts a single stroke that was not in the last year, and accepts diabetes.
options.why: Correct. At 18 months, one stroke, he fits.

options.t: Foresters would decline him for the stroke.
options.why: Foresters lists a stroke within 2 years as its Standard Death Benefit, not a decline.

options.t: Mutual of Omaha Living Promise would be graded, since the stroke was within 2 years.
options.why: Correct. Good to know when comparing.

options.t: AIG SIWL is out. It declines anyone who has had a stroke and also has diabetes.
options.why: Correct. The combination is a decline at AIG, regardless of timing.

options.t: Mutual of Omaha Term Life Express is a good fit.
options.why: Term Life Express declines stroke.

options.t: Royal Neighbors accepts a stroke after one year, and diabetes without insulin.
options.why: Correct. Another level option.

title: Home From the Hospital
file: Three nights in the hospital for pneumonia, discharged five weeks ago. Fully recovered
High blood pressure, controlled on one medication
story: Wanda mentions the hospital stay as if it barely counts: "It was just pneumonia. I am fine now."
prompt: Work out how you would handle it. Choose what to ask, which carrier fits, and what to tell her.

groups.label: What to ask first
groups.hint: Pick the two questions that decide which carriers are open to her.

options.t: Whether she liked her doctor.
options.why: Friendly, but not underwriting.

options.t: The exact admission and discharge dates.
options.why: Several carriers look back exactly 12 months, and some count nights or days.

options.t: The reason for the stay, and whether she is fully recovered or still being treated.
options.why: A finished stay is treated very differently from a current one.

options.t: Whether she would rather leave it off the application.
options.why: Suggesting she leave it off invites misrepresentation.

options.t: Which hospital she was in.
options.why: Can help with records, but it does not change which carriers fit.

options.t: Nothing. One short stay does not matter.
options.why: It matters a lot at some carriers.

groups.label: Which carrier fits
groups.hint: Pick the choice that matches our guide.

options.t: Transamerica FE Express.
options.why: FE Express declines two or more nights in the hospital within 12 months.

options.t: Guaranteed issue, to be safe.
options.why: Unnecessary. She would take a waiting period she does not need.

options.t: Mutual of Omaha Living Promise.
options.why: Living Promise declines a hospital stay within the last 12 months.

options.t: A carrier that does not penalize a finished short stay, such as Americo (declines only a current stay) or LBL (declines only more than 5 days in the last year).
options.why: Correct. Three nights, finished five weeks ago, fits both.

groups.label: What to tell her
groups.hint: Pick the explanation that is honest and keeps her trust.

options.t: "The stay will not matter anywhere."
options.why: False. It would matter at several carriers.

options.t: "Come back in a year and we will try then."
options.why: Leaves her uncovered when good options exist now.

options.t: Say nothing and submit.
options.why: She deserves to know why you chose that carrier.

options.t: "Some companies look back 12 months at hospital stays, so I will match you with one that fits. Every answer still needs to be exact."
options.why: Honest, reassuring, and it keeps the application accurate.

title: Help With Bathing
file: Arthritis and heart trouble. Her daughter helps her bathe and dress every day
Enough to cover a simple funeral
story: Her daughter mentions the daily help while making coffee. Josephine waves it off: "That is just family helping out."
prompt: What does this mean for underwriting per our guide?

options.t: Americo will accept her, since arthritis and a stable heart condition are both acceptable and the help at home is only from family.
options.why: Americo declines when someone needs help with activities of daily living.

options.t: Only mention it if the application specifically asks about wheelchairs or nursing homes, since family helping out is not a medical condition.
options.why: Help with bathing and dressing is an activities of daily living question. Hiding it can void the policy.

options.t: Needing help with daily living is a decline at nearly every carrier on our guide, but Royal Neighbors lists it under guaranteed issue. That is the honest path, with its waiting period explained.
options.why: Correct. You found the real path and set honest expectations, instead of a decline or a bad claim later.

options.t: Foresters Plan Right at the Preferred level, since the daily help comes from her daughter rather than a nurse or home health aide, and Foresters only asks about paid care and nursing facilities.
options.why: Foresters declines when someone needs help with activities of daily living.

title: Running the Health Interview
file: Place the client with the right carrier and plan on the first try, with an application that holds up at claim time
story: A clean health interview avoids surprise declines, wrong plan tiers and claims that get denied later. The order you do it in matters.
prompt: Put these steps in the order you would use them.

steps.t: Check the conditions and medications against the underwriting guide and each carrier's drug list
steps.why: This is where you find which carriers accept, grade or decline.

steps.t: Ask about each diagnosis, hospital stay and surgery, with dates
steps.why: Timing drives most underwriting rules: within 1, 2 or 4 years.

steps.t: Go through every medication, bottle in hand, with the dose and what each one is for
steps.why: Medications reveal conditions clients forget to mention.

steps.t: Explain why you ask health questions, and that honest answers are what make the claim pay
steps.why: Clients answer more completely when they know why it matters.

steps.t: Complete the application's health questions exactly as the client answered them
steps.why: Accurate answers protect the claim.

steps.t: Choose the carrier and plan tier that fit, and explain why to the client
steps.why: The client should understand why they are getting level or graded coverage.

title: What Is the Gabapentin For?
file: "The gabapentin is for my feet. They tingle."
story: Leonard reads his bottles off one at a time. He did not mention nerve problems when you asked about his health.
prompt: What does the gabapentin tell you per our guide?

options.t: Skip it on the application, since he did not mention any nerve problems when you asked about his health conditions.
options.why: The medication shows a condition he did not list. It has to be accounted for.

options.t: Note it as being for seizures, since Foresters gives gabapentin for seizures its Preferred Death Benefit, which gets him the best rate, and he never actually mentioned neuropathy by name.
options.why: He told you it is for his feet. Assuming a better reason is not honest underwriting.

options.t: Gabapentin is a common pain medication many seniors take for aches, so it does not change anything as long as he lists it.
options.why: At several carriers, why he takes it changes the outcome.

options.t: With metformin, it likely means diabetic nerve pain. Mutual of Omaha declines gabapentin with diabetes and Foresters grades neuropathy, while Transamerica Immediate Solution accepts it.
options.why: Correct. Asking what each medication is for turned a routine bottle into the key underwriting fact.

title: Edibles, Not Cigarettes
file: Marijuana edibles a few nights a week, legal in her state. No tobacco
story: Pam asks, a little embarrassed, "Does the marijuana make me a smoker?"
prompt: What rate class should you expect per our guide?

options.t: Tobacco rates at every carrier, since insurance companies treat any marijuana use the same way they treat cigarettes.
options.why: Not per our guide, and it would overcharge her.

options.t: Non-tobacco rates. Mutual of Omaha accepts marijuana at non-smoker rates, and Foresters gives non-tobacco Preferred when it is legal in her state (vaping is tobacco rates there).
options.why: Correct. The details, legal in her state and edibles rather than vaping, get her the better rate.

options.t: She does not need to mention it, since edibles are not smoking, the tobacco question only asks about cigarettes and cigars, and marijuana is fully legal in the state where she lives now.
options.why: If the application asks, it must be answered honestly.

options.t: She will be declined at most carriers, since regular marijuana use counts as drug use on the health questions.
options.why: Wrong. Marijuana use is accepted at the carriers that list it.

title: Outside the Build Chart
file: Otherwise healthy. High blood pressure, controlled
story: Denise is healthy apart from her weight, and she is self-conscious about it.
prompt: What is the smart underwriting move per our guide?

options.t: Check her height and weight against each carrier's build chart first. If she falls outside most of them, Royal Neighbors and CVS do not use a build chart on our guide.
options.why: Correct. Build rules out a healthy client more often than agents expect, and these two carriers skip the chart.

options.t: Go straight to guaranteed issue so she does not have to discuss her weight at all, since she is clearly self-conscious about it and the plan still covers a simple funeral.
options.why: Kind in intent, but it gives a healthy client a waiting period she may not need.

options.t: Weight only matters for term insurance, so it will not affect a final expense plan for someone who is otherwise healthy.
options.why: Most final expense carriers on our guide use a build chart.

options.t: Round her weight down a little to fit the chart, since a few pounds either way is within normal scale error anyway.
options.why: Misrepresentation. It can void the policy.

title: A-Fib and a Blood Thinner
file: A-fib diagnosed 3 years ago. Takes a blood thinner every day
story: Harriet is proud that her A-fib has been stable for years and expects to qualify anywhere.
prompt: Which statement is accurate per our guide?

options.t: Mutual of Omaha Living Promise with a full benefit from day one, since her A-fib was diagnosed more than 2 years ago, has been stable ever since, and Living Promise accepts A-fib over 2 years.
options.why: Living Promise accepts A-fib over 2 years, but declines blood thinners.

options.t: Have her ask her doctor about stopping the blood thinner before she applies, so she can qualify with more carriers.
options.why: Never steer medical decisions for underwriting. It is unsafe and unethical.

options.t: Mutual of Omaha Living Promise would decline her for the blood thinner, but Americo, Royal Neighbors and CVS accept A-fib, and AIG SIWL lists A-fib on a daily blood thinner as level.
options.why: Correct. The medication, not just the diagnosis, decides the carrier.

options.t: A-fib is a heart rhythm condition, so she should expect graded coverage with a waiting period at every carrier on our guide.
options.why: Not per our guide. Several carriers accept her.

title: Dialysis Three Days a Week
file: Kidney dialysis for the past 2 years
Something so his wife is not left with the funeral bill
story: Curtis has been turned down twice and says, "Nobody takes dialysis patients."
prompt: Which response is accurate per our guide?

options.t: He is right. Dialysis is a decline at every carrier on our guide, so the kindest thing is to be honest with him, not waste his time, and suggest he set money aside in savings instead.
options.why: Not per our guide. There are two paths to check.

options.t: Mutual of Omaha Living Promise with a graded benefit, since his dialysis started more than a year ago.
options.why: Living Promise declines dialysis.

options.t: Americo will accept him, since it accepts most kidney conditions, including chronic kidney disease.
options.why: Americo declines dialysis.

options.t: Most carriers on our guide decline dialysis, but Transamerica FE Express accepts it after 12 months (Select on our guide), and Royal Neighbors has guaranteed issue.
options.why: Correct. Knowing the exceptions can get coverage for someone who has already been turned down.

title: Why Do You Need My Pill Bottles?
file: "Why do you need to see all my pill bottles? That feels a little personal."
story: Beverly is friendly but guarded. She hands you one bottle and keeps the rest in the bag.
prompt: Write what you would say, in 2 to 5 sentences. Explain why the medications matter, in a way that earns her trust.

rubric.label: Acknowledges her feeling
rubric.tip: Respect the concern before you explain.

rubric.label: Explains it helps find the right company or plan
rubric.tip: Show her how it helps her, not just the paperwork.

rubric.label: Explains that accurate answers protect the claim
rubric.tip: This is the most important reason, for her family.

rubric.label: Reassures her about privacy
rubric.tip: People share more when they know where it goes.

rubric.label: Invites her to continue
rubric.tip: End with a question that brings her back in.

sample: That is a fair question, and I understand it feels personal. Your medications help me match you with the right company, so you get the best plan and price you qualify for. They also make sure your answers are exact, which is what protects the claim for your family. It stays private and is only used for your application. Would it be okay if we went through them together?
